claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is predominantly controlled by the dynamic interplay between mechanical film removal and in situ re-passivation.
Sliding mechanically disrupts or removes the protective oxide film.
Mechanical film disruption transiently exposes bare alloy and accelerates corrosion.
The passive film rapidly reforms after sliding damage and restores corrosion protection.
Transient passive-layer integrity is the structural mediator governing coupled wear-corrosion behavior.
The tested specimen will have a smooth, chemically homogeneous surface with an intact passive oxide film.
An in situ tribo-electrochemical cell with imaging, friction monitoring, and electrochemical monitoring will be used.
The comparison will systematically vary normal load and sliding speed.
Chloride-containing solutions such as NaCl are aggressive corrosive environments capable of affecting passive films.
Increasing mechanical load or sliding velocity will increase oxide-film disruption.
Film-disruption events will produce transient spikes in electrochemical current.
Greater localized surface damage will correlate with a higher friction coefficient.
Increasing load or sliding velocity will cause a nonlinear increase in total degradation relative to a static or low-wear baseline.
Under mild mechanical conditions, rapid passive-film repair will mitigate total degradation.
A static-corrosion or low-load, low-speed baseline will retain a largely undisturbed passive film and exhibit low degradation.
The proposed mechanism should govern when re-passivation is fast enough to recover the film between wear events.
The mechanism may cease to govern when mechanical stress permanently prevents film recovery or when re-passivation is sluggish.
Passive-film behavior varies among high-entropy-alloy compositions.
Film integrity, electrochemical current and potential, friction coefficient, and wear-track morphology will be measured during the controlled comparison.

Absence of correlation between mechanically induced film disruption and transient electrochemical-current increases, or persistence of an intact film under mechanical challenge, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
